exercise1.prompt: Merging on a Key: Keep everyone, count the gaps
exercise1.hint: how="left" keeps every person. The people who matched nothing have a missing score, and isna().sum() counts them.

exercise2.prompt: Merging on a Key: Inner against left, as a pair

hiddenCases.name: a complete match makes the two equal
a duplicate on the right multiplies both

exercise2.hint: Two merges, one with the default how and one with how="left", and len() on each. When the two numbers differ, the difference is how many left rows matched nothing.

questions.prompt: What does an inner join keep?
choices: Only rows whose key is in both tables
questions.explain: Which quietly changes the question from "each person" to "each person who also appears in the other file".

questions.prompt: Which join keeps every row of the left table?
questions.explain: Rows with no partner get NaN in the columns that came from the right.

questions.prompt: After a left join, what identifies the rows that matched nothing?
choices: NaN in a column that came from the right
questions.explain: isna().sum() on one of those columns counts them, and that number is usually worth reporting.

questions.prompt: An inner join returns fewer rows than the left table. What does that mean?
questions.explain: Worth checking rather than accepting — the cause is often a type mismatch rather than genuinely absent data.
